components.text: Challenges the required first-stage assumption that reality contains genuinely contingent things.
It challenges the required antecedent by demanding proof that anything is genuinely modally contingent.
Identifies the objection's conflation of causal determination with metaphysical necessity.
Preserves the further explanatory question why the determining system exists.
It directly denies that causal determination should be conflated with metaphysical necessary existence.
It notes that the determining machine's own existence remains open to explanation.
The modal demand to establish that apparently contingent things could have been otherwise.
Offers independent support for seeking explanations of contingent existence.
It supports inquiry into contingent existence through induction, scientific practice, and observed order.
It acknowledges that applying the generalization to a totality raises a composition issue.
Replaces an exclusively modal demand with a distinction between possible nonexistence and existential dependence.
Concedes that modal contingency remains one legitimate sense of the term.
It directly clarifies that modal contingency and existential dependence are distinct concepts.
It indicates that either concept may figure in versions of a contingency argument.
Rejects determination as sufficient to explain why the determined thing or arrangement exists.
Does not independently prove that the determined outcome could have been otherwise.
It argues that determination does not answer why the determined thing or determining structure exists.
It characterizes bare appeal to being determined as circular rather than explanatory.
Demands a relevant distinction between God's stopping point and comparable non-divine stopping points.
Questions whether necessary existence alone warrants identifying the terminus as God.
It applies the proponent's rejection of unexplained stopping points to the proposed necessary God.
It challenges whether calling the necessary terminus God supplies any asymmetric explanatory advantage.
Introduces the stronger case where a necessary antecedent necessarily produces each subsequent effect.
Argues that the complete necessary chain removes contingency rather than merely explaining an outcome.
It supplies the stronger conditional under which necessary causation would propagate through every effect.
It maintains that tracing the chain backward may yield necessary events rather than contingent ones.
Challenges consistency between rejecting self-causation and allowing God to terminate explanation.
Argues that labeling God non-contingent does not by itself exempt God from explanatory scrutiny.
It tests whether the rejection of self-causation is consistently applied to the proposed God.
It argues that an unexplained God would not complete the identification-stage explanatory burden.
Challenges the move from explanations of each contingent member to explanation of the complete collection.
Questions whether a further totality-level explanation is required once members are explained.
It challenges extending explanatory requirements from each contingent member to their complete collection.
It distinguishes member-level unanswered questions from the separate claim that the group needs explanation.
Recasts all contingent things as a plurality rather than an additional composed object.
Argues that member-level explanations leave why this plurality exists unanswered.
It reframes the subject as a plurality rather than a further composed object and preserves a residual why-question.
It argues that separate member explanations do not explain why this plurality rather than none or another plurality exists.
Challenges the assumption that distinct member explanations converge upon one external source.
Raises the alternative of separate explanatory chains that do not converge.
It argues that the factory illustration presupposes convergence on one ultimate explanatory source.
It identifies the alternative of separate explanatory chains that need not converge.
Offers the universe itself as a necessary terminus if genuine contingency has not been established.
Treats determinism as potentially eliminating contingency throughout the universe.
It denies the need for an external explanation if the universe contains no genuinely contingent things.
It treats determinism as potentially supporting the necessary-universe alternative.
Demands an argument connecting necessary existence to a distinct perfect being with divine attributes.
Concedes at most a necessary foundation while disputing its identification as God.
It directly demands the missing bridge from necessary reality to a distinct being with divine attributes.
It distinguishes an external necessary explanation from the stronger perfect-being conclusion.
Proposes an abductive comparison to support the perfect-being identification over a necessary universe.
Treats the necessary-universe view as a rival hypothesis to be compared.
It proposes filling the attributes gap by abductively comparing perfect-being and necessary-universe hypotheses.
It accepts the necessary-universe hypothesis as a rival to be compared on explanatory virtues.
Requires the abductive comparison to make God more compelling than the necessary-universe rival.
Explains that parity cannot justify the specifically theistic conclusion.
It states that parity between the rival hypotheses cannot support the specifically theistic conclusion.
It requires the proponent to show that God is more compelling than the universe.
Offers maximal simplicity and resulting intrinsic probability as a comparative advantage for a perfect being.
Uses perfection as part of a substantive hypothesis rather than a bare label.
It supplies simplicity and prior probability as reasons to prefer the perfect-being hypothesis.
It identifies maximal simplicity as a feature of the proposed perfect being.
Claims that a perfect being avoids arbitrary finite limits afflicting rival necessary foundations.
Challenges limited non-divine foundations by asking what explains their specific capacities.
It offers absence of arbitrary finite creative limits as a comparative advantage for a perfect being.
It argues that a finitely powerful necessary foundation would generate another unexplained contrast.
Counters that simple mathematical laws may be less complex than a God possessing a will.
Argues that divine will introduces further contingency and dependence questions.
Performs a direct explanatory-economy comparison with the necessary-universe rival.
It directly contests the claim that a willing God is simpler than a universe governed by mathematical laws.
It argues that divine will introduces dependence and contingency questions of its own.
It performs the requested rival comparison on explanatory economy.
